summaries.example: Imagine a sheet showing the paths that moving objects can take. In an ordinary sheet, a path keeps going forward without meeting itself. A strange change to the sheet could make one path loop around and meet its own earlier part. A Thornian time machine would be something that causes this change. It is not simply a box with a date dial.
summaries.summary: The entry studies a scientific idea that is different from the usual movie time machine. A Thornian time machine is a device or process that changes spacetime so that closed timelike curves, or looping paths through time, appear. The discussion begins with a quiet past in which no such loops exist. It then asks whether later loops can fairly be blamed on what the machine did. This is difficult because general relativity may allow more than one later development from the same earlier situation. The entry reviews possible no-go results in classical general relativity and in quantum approaches to gravity. Some results depend on special assumptions about energy, horizons, or the absence of “holes” in spacetime. Those assumptions and their physical importance remain unsettled. The main conclusion is careful: no conclusive no-go theorem currently shows that every Thornian time machine is impossible. Even if machines can never work, studying them can teach us about time, cause and effect, spacetime, and the basic laws of gravity.
key_ideas: Physics usually describes time travel using looping paths in spacetime, not mainly with story puzzles such as changing your grandfather’s past.
A Thornian time machine would change the shape of spacetime so that these looping paths appear.
Scientists and philosophers have found arguments against some time machines, but the entry says there is not yet one final proof that rules them all out.
A major problem is deciding when a machine really caused the loops, especially if the earlier state does not completely determine what happens later.
summaries.why_it_matters: Time machines sound like pure science fiction, but studying them tests serious ideas about how the universe works. The question connects to whether the future is fixed, whether unusual spacetime shapes can form, and how general relativity might fit with quantum physics. It also shows why scientists must define an idea clearly before trying to prove that it is possible or impossible.

important_terms.definition: A possible path through spacetime that always moves toward the future but eventually returns to an event on the same path.
A device or process that creates closed timelike curves where there were none before.
A mathematical result showing that a proposed kind of machine cannot work if certain starting rules and physical conditions hold.
The idea that later events are fixed by earlier conditions and the laws of nature.

questions_to_think_about: Would a machine count as a time machine if loops appeared nearby but the machine did not clearly cause them?
Is a story puzzle about changing the past the same problem as proving that a machine can be built?
Why might scientists study an impossible machine?
What kinds of evidence would make you trust a no-go result?

summaries.example: Suppose a relativistic model has a partial Cauchy surface Σ₀: an earlier spacelike slice with no closed timelike curves to its past. Later, a chronology-violating region V contains such curves. If every physically acceptable, hole-free extension of the future development of Σ₀ contains CTCs, one might say the initial setup is responsible for producing them. But if there is another equally acceptable extension with no future CTCs, the claim that a machine produced them is weakened. This illustrates why the debate is not settled merely by finding one spacetime containing loops.
summaries.summary:
“Time machine” has two importantly different meanings. A Wellsian machine transports an operator to a selected date, whereas the physics literature examined here focuses on a Thornian machine: a device or process that brings about closed timelike curves (CTCs) in a spacetime that previously had none. A CTC is a future-directed timelike worldline that closes back on itself. Thus, the relevant question is not primarily whether a traveler can create a grandfather paradox. It is whether a process can generate a region of spacetime with CTCs and whether the earlier state can be regarded as responsible for that generation.

To formulate that question, one starts with a partial Cauchy surface Σ₀ whose past contains no CTCs. The later chronology-violating region lies beyond the future domain of dependence of Σ₀, so ordinary causal determinism does not guarantee that the initial state fixes the later CTCs. Various weaker responsibility conditions are considered. Compact generation of the future Cauchy horizon is one candidate: roughly, its past-directed null generators remain within a bounded region. This excludes some artificial examples and implies a breakdown of strong causality near the horizon, but it may not be a necessary feature of every possible machine. The discussion also examines extensions, maximality, and “hole-free” conditions. A central possibility is that every suitable, hole-free extension of the initial development contains future CTCs; if so, the initial setup could plausibly be credited with producing them. Results showing that some extensions avoid CTCs therefore matter, but they do not automatically settle the debate unless the relevant assumptions are physically justified.

key_ideas: The entry distinguishes Wellsian time machines, which resemble familiar science fiction devices, from Thornian machines, which operate by altering spacetime geometry so CTCs emerge.
Time-travel paradoxes are not the central test for a Thornian machine. The key issue comes earlier: whether a device can produce the spacetime structure containing CTCs.
Causal determinism is too strong or otherwise unavailable in the relevant setting, because a CTC region can lie beyond the future domain of dependence of the initial surface.
Proposed criteria such as compactly generated Cauchy horizons can exclude some models and support chronology-protection results, but their status as necessary conditions for a machine is disputed.

In classical general relativity, Hawking-style results restrict some open-universe cases under the weak energy condition, yet they do not settle all cases, including relevant closed-universe possibilities.

Quantum field effects can threaten or disrupt some chronology horizons, but semiclassical results rely on assumptions and may break down where full quantum gravity is needed. Existing quantum-gravity programs do not yet provide a conclusive general verdict.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic is a concentrated case study in how physics and philosophy interact. It raises questions about causation when determinism fails, about which mathematical models represent physically possible worlds, and about how to interpret the boundaries of a theory. The search for time-machine impossibility results also bears on cosmic censorship, chronology protection, and attempts to construct a quantum theory of gravity. Even a final negative answer would be informative if it explained which fundamental principles block the machines.

important_terms.definition: A smooth, future-directed timelike worldline that eventually intersects itself; in the physics literature, it represents a possible route through spacetime that returns to an earlier event on the route.
A device or process that changes spacetime so that CTCs arise where they did not previously exist; this is the technical focus of the entry.
A spacelike slice used to describe initial conditions, with a causal-development region determined by those conditions under the relevant equations.
The boundary beyond which the state is not uniquely fixed by data on a chosen partial Cauchy surface.
A theorem intended to show that, given specified physical assumptions, a time machine cannot operate.
A condition intended to exclude problematic extensions of spacetime that contain missing regions or analogous structural defects.
The view that CTCs do not arise under physically reasonable conditions, or arise only in highly non-generic cases.
A broad conjecture that physically reasonable conditions prevent certain severe spacetime pathologies, including some forms of singular or acausal behavior.

questions_to_think_about: If several physically allowed futures fit the same initial data, what kind of responsibility could a machine have for the CTCs in one future?
Should a condition used in a no-go theorem count as decisive if it has not been shown to be necessary for every Thornian machine?
Could ruling out spacetime holes simply replace a time-machine problem with a hole-machine problem?
Why might the failure of semiclassical quantum gravity near a chronology horizon be a limitation of the approximation rather than a proof that CTCs are impossible?
What would count as a physically reasonable restriction on possible spacetime models?

summaries.example: Picture a video game world whose map normally lets every path move forward without looping back. A game designer might change the map so that a path eventually returns to an earlier place in its own route. If the change happened after a special machine was activated, we might call the machine a Thornian time machine. But suppose the game’s rules allow several different maps to grow from the same starting screen. One map has loops and another does not. Then it is hard to say that the starting screen forced the machine’s result. This is the entry’s problem about responsibility.
summaries.summary:
The SEP entry examines whether physics permits a particular kind of time machine. The familiar science-fiction version lets someone select a date and travel there. The technical version, associated with work by Kip Thorne and others, is different: it would alter the geometry of spacetime so that closed timelike curves appear. A closed timelike curve is a possible route that always moves forward in its local time direction but eventually loops back to an earlier event on the route.

The entry says that the famous time-travel puzzles are not the main obstacle to these machines. Those puzzles concern what happens after CTCs already exist. The physics debate instead asks whether a machine can produce them and whether the earlier conditions can be held responsible. That second question is difficult because the equations of general relativity do not always make the future uniquely determined by data on an earlier slice. The CTC region may lie beyond a Cauchy horizon, where the initial information no longer controls one unique continuation. Researchers therefore consider weaker ideas of responsibility, such as requiring CTCs to arise in every acceptable continuation of the earlier state.

The entry reviews examples and proposed restrictions in classical general relativity. Conditions involving compactly generated horizons, energy requirements, determinism, and hole-free spacetime extensions can exclude some candidates or create no-go arguments. However, the authors emphasize that a condition may be useful without yet being proved necessary for every possible machine. Hawking’s chronology-protection work limits certain cases, especially under specified assumptions, but does not settle all spatial settings. Quantum field theory and semiclassical gravity add further complications
key_ideas: The technical debate is about making CTCs, not about a traveler using a machine to dial a date as in science-fiction stories.
A CTC would make a possible observer’s route return to an earlier event, but that does not by itself show that a machine created the route.
The central philosophical difficulty is causal responsibility: the earlier state may not determine the later spacetime once a horizon is reached.
Some mathematical results rule out machines only after adding assumptions about energy, the shape of a horizon, or acceptable spacetime extensions.
Classical general relativity gives important restrictions, but the entry says these restrictions do not amount to a conclusive ban on every Thornian machine.
Quantum effects may disrupt the formation of CTCs, yet current approaches to quantum gravity are not developed enough to give a final answer.
summaries.why_it_matters: This question matters because it links an exciting idea to serious questions about cause and effect. It asks whether the laws of nature allow unusual spacetime shapes, whether the future is fixed by the past, and whether mathematical models with odd features should count as physically possible. The topic also helps researchers explore the foundations of relativity and the search for quantum gravity.

important_terms.definition: A path through spacetime that always points toward the future but eventually comes back to meet itself.
A process that changes spacetime so that closed timelike curves appear; this is the kind of machine studied by the physics literature.
A proposed proof that something cannot happen when certain rules or assumptions are accepted.
The view that earlier conditions and physical laws fix what happens later.
A boundary separating the region fixed by earlier data from a region where that data does not uniquely determine the future.
A proposed rule that excludes spacetime models with certain missing or defective extensions.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between a world containing CTCs and a machine that causes CTCs?
If the same starting conditions can lead to different futures, can we still call one future the result of a machine?
Why might a theorem be impressive but still not settle the whole question?
Would a rule excluding “holes” in spacetime be a physical law, a mathematical preference, or both?
What could scientists learn from studying something they may never build?
